steps.title: Basic Troubleshooting
steps.markdownContent:
What happens when your circuit doesn't work? Don't worry—every engineer runs into bugs! You just need to become an **Engineering Detective**! 🕵️

### The 3 Clues to Check:
1. **Check Power**: Is the little green light labeled **'ON'** lit on the Arduino? If not, check if the USB cable is firmly plugged in.
2. **Check the Pin Match**: Look at your code. Did the code command **Pin 13**, but the wire is plugged into **Pin 12**? If the pins don't match, the signal won't reach your part!
3. **Check Ground (GND)**: Is the ground wire securely plugged in? Remember, electricity can't flow without a complete return path.

Let's learn the detective strategies used by master engineers to solve any hardware bug!

quickCheck.question: If an LED light does not turn on, what is the best first thing to check?
options: Check that wires are plugged into the right pins and firmly connected
Throw all the parts into the trash
Paint the wires with colorful glitter
quickCheck.explanation: Checking that wires are firmly connected to the correct pins fixes most electronics puzzles!
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: When something doesn't work, stay calm and check connections first: are wires in the right spots?

quickCheck.question: If your code commands Pin 13, but your wire is plugged into Pin 8, what will happen?
options: The part on Pin 8 will not receive the command
The computer will turn into a pumpkin
Pin 8 will automatically slide over to Pin 13
quickCheck.explanation: Code commands specific pins! If the wire is plugged into the wrong pin, the signal won't reach it.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Code and wires must match! If code commands Pin 13, the wire must be connected to Pin 13.

steps.title: The Hardware Detective's Playbook
steps.markdownContent:
### The Top 4 Rookie Hardware Traps 🛠️

When a circuit goes silent, run through this 4-step diagnostic checklist:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. THE POWER CHECK (Green 'ON' LED)                     │
│    Is board powered? USB cable seated firmly?           │
│                                                         │
│ 2. THE PIN MISMATCH (Code vs Wire)                      │
│    Code: digitalWrite(13, HIGH);                        │
│    Wire: Plugged into Pin 12 by accident! (Mismatch!)   │
│                                                         │
│ 3. THE MISSING GROUND (Open Circuit)                    │
│    Is GND plugged in? Electrons must return home!       │
│                                                         │
│ 4. REVERSED POLARITY (Directional Components)           │
│    LED long leg (Anode +) vs short leg (Cathode - GND)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Diagnostic Strategy:
- **Rule of One Change**: Only change ONE wire or ONE line of code at a time! If you change 5 things at once, you won't know which fix actually worked.
- **Physical Feel**: Gently wiggle jumper wires—loose breadboard spring clips cause 80% of intermittent bugs.

steps.title: Interactive Troubleshooting Bench
steps.markdownContent:
### Mission: The Silent LED Mystery! 🔍

A fellow monster engineer built a circuit, but the test LED refuses to light up!
1. Inspect the code: The sketch commands `digitalWrite(13, HIGH);`
2. Inspect the board: Where is the red jumper wire currently plugged in?
3. Select your diagnosis from the choices.
4. Move the wire to the correct pin to repair the circuit and verify operation!

steps.title: Troubleshooting Master Checkpoint
steps.markdownContent: Test your hardware troubleshooting instincts and detective skills!

interactiveConfig.question: Why should an engineer change only ONE thing at a time when debugging a circuit?
options: So you know exactly which change solved the problem or caused a new issue
Because changing two wires makes the board explode
To make the troubleshooting take longer
interactiveConfig.explanation: Changing one variable at a time isolate causes, ensuring clear and repeatable engineering solutions.

options: So you know exactly which change solved the problem or caused a new issue

questions.explanation: Changing one variable at a time isolate causes, ensuring clear and repeatable engineering solutions.

questions.question: What is the very first clue to check if an Arduino project does nothing at all?
options: Check if the green 'ON' power LED on the board is illuminated
Unscrew all screws on the table
questions.explanation: If the green 'ON' LED is unlit, the Arduino has no electrical power, so no code can run.

questions.question: If your code commands Pin 9 to turn HIGH, but your wire is in Pin 8, what happens?
options: The component on Pin 8 receives nothing because the commanded pin does not match
The Arduino moves the wire automatically
questions.explanation: Software commands specific physical pins. If code and wiring mismatch, signals cannot reach their target.
